abstract: This Master's dissertation (written in Portuguese at the Federal University of Bahia) investigates whether the use of digital platforms alters the work relations and practices of independent professional tattoo artists, focusing on their use of Instagram. Adopting a neo-materialist, less anthropocentric lens, it treats Instagram as an agent whose material tools and algorithmic performativity 'make-do' and reshape tattooing work. Drawing on an autoethnography of the author's own tattoo practice and a survey of 590 tattoo artists, it concludes that Instagram use generates dependence and transforms the social profile of workers, their workspaces, procedures, unpaid work hours, and may turn tattoo artists into influencers and products.
key_claims: Digital platforms possess agency and, in association with their users, co-produce and modify the social world of work through their materiality and algorithmic performativity.

Even professions that pre-date and do not originally depend on digital platforms (such as tattooing on Instagram) can become so intertwined with a platform that they generate dependence and significant changes, fitting the concept of platformized work.

Instagram use 'tattoos the tattoo artists' — adding new tasks to their routine, altering temporal regimes, modifying the tattooing procedure, reconfiguring the workspace, and changing the profile of who can be a tattoo artist.
The platformization of work should be understood less as 'uberization' and more as the dependence that workers and consumers develop on digital platforms.

To gain professional advantage, tattoo artists must 'play the platform's game' — adapting to its algorithmic logic and feeding it content, thereby performing unpaid labor that generates data and profit for Instagram.
methods: Neo-materialist methodological approach to social studies of communication (drawing on Lemos, Alldred & Fox, Coole & Frost), treating the platform as a non-human agent.
Descriptive analysis of Instagram's visible tools, features, account types, interface, materiality, and algorithmic performativity based on the platform's own official documentation.
Autoethnography: critical self-analysis of the author's own professional Instagram account and tattooing practice over a defined period, examined under a less anthropocentric perspective.
Online survey (questionnaire) with 590 tattoo artist respondents about their Instagram use and perceptions of how it shapes their professional practice.
Comparison and triangulation of survey data with the autoethnographic findings.
findings: The use of Instagram generates dependence among tattoo artists and alters their social profile, workspace, activities, procedures, and unpaid work hours.

Tattoo artists reconfigure their physical workspaces to make them 'Instagrammable' (standardized photographic backgrounds, decoration, dedicated image-capture areas) and adopt practices that strengthen a visual identity.
The tattooing procedure itself is modified by the integration of smartphones (e.g., documenting steps, techniques to arouse curiosity, partially covering tattoos with gifs).
Platform use adds unpaid labor to the routine (portfolio curation, client communication, learning the platform) that is often not perceived as work because it blends with leisure.

Most survey perceptions matched the autoethnography; unexpected results pointed strongly to platform-driven changes, including surveillance and the potential transformation of tattoo artists into digital influencers and products, with symptoms of work precarization.
Platform success depends on the degree to which artists adapt to Instagram's algorithmic functioning and feed it content.
contributions: Proposes an addition to existing typologies of platformized work: a category of freelance professionals who use digital social networks (not designed for work) as work platforms — e.g., tattoo artists, confectioners, psychologists, hairdressers, influencers.
Extends the concept of platformization of work beyond app-based couriers/drivers ('uberization') to self-employed creative professionals on social media.
Provides an empirical case study (autoethnography plus a 590-respondent survey) documenting how Instagram materially shapes an analog, pre-digital craft profession.
Offers a methodological template for neo-materialist studies of how digital platforms affect specific professional fields among independent workers.
framing: The dissertation positions itself within neo-materialist social studies of communication (Lemos; Alldred & Fox; Coole & Frost), emphasizing non-human agency and the 'make-do' capacity of technical objects. It engages the literatures on digital platforms and the platformization/uberization of labor (Grohmann, Casilli & Posada, Scholz, Fuchs & Sevignani, D'Andrea & Guerra, the ILO) to analyze precarization and unpaid digital labor among independent workers.
